1037.title: Al-Aqsa in Jerusalem
1037.hook: the farthest mosque in Jerusalem, named third in the hadith of the three mosques
1037.howItsDone: Muslims who can travel to Jerusalem often pray at al-Aqsa, and those who cannot remember it in their prayers and in the story of the Night Journey, recited from Surah al-Isra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, raised beside his home, where he now rests, near the Rawdah. Your line was his mosque. Did a blessing on him cross your lips? Day one thousand thirty-seven.

On a wide stone platform in the Old City of Jerusalem, two buildings catch the light. One wears a golden dome; we met it months back, the Dome of the Rock, a shrine built over the rock. The other is lower and longer, at the southern end, with a plainer gray dome. The gold tends to steal the eye. But the long building at the far end is where the rows form on a Friday, shoulder to shoulder, facing south toward Mecca. Its name comes straight out of a verse of the Qur'an. Today: Al-Aqsa in Jerusalem.
screen: `ONE PLATFORM, TWO BUILDINGS.` → `THE GOLD DOME IS THE SHRINE.` → `THE ROWS FORM AT THE FAR END.`

segments.voice: Start with the verse. Surah seventeen opens with the Night Journey of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In Pickthall's translation, God carried His servant by night "from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship." The Inviolable one is the mosque in Mecca. The Far Distant one, in Arabic al-masjid al-aqsa, is the farthest mosque. The verse gave the place its name. Notice what the verse leaves out: it never names Jerusalem. Muslims have understood the Far Distant place as the mosque there. Second, the list we heard two days ago. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says not to set out on a special journey except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the Prophet's own mosque in Medina, and al-Aqsa. Jerusalem is named third, and this week has walked them in that order. Third, an older link. Another hadith tells of a companion, Abu Dharr, who asked which mosque was set up first on earth. The answer: the Sacred Mosque. And then? Al-Aqsa. The two are paired from the start. Fourth, the name stretches. Some people use al-Aqsa for the long prayer hall alone. Others use it for the whole walled enclosure, courtyards, trees, the Dome of the Rock and all, which is also called the Noble Sanctuary. The same hill is holy to Jews, who call it the Temple Mount, and the city is dear to Christians. A crowded holiness, and a reason people of more than one faith pray for its peace.
screen: `THE FAR DISTANT PLACE OF WORSHIP.` · `THE THIRD OF THREE MOSQUES.` · `PAIRED WITH MECCA FROM THE START.` · `A HALL, OR THE WHOLE SANCTUARY.` · then, large: `THE FARTHEST MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: The practice: hold Jerusalem in mind for two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Let the city come to you as a place, not a headline: stone streets, bells and calls to prayer, families buying bread, children on their way to school, worshippers of more than one faith passing in the same lanes. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for peace and safety for Jerusalem and everyone who lives there. If you don't, simply wish them well, one face at a time. The bell holds the time.
Al-Aqsa, the farthest mosque named in the Qur'an's verse of the Night Journey, and third in the hadith of the three mosques. Today's word.
Your line: the farthest mosque. Today, when you hear Jerusalem in the news, stop for one breath and wish the whole city peace before you scroll on. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

1038.title: Mosques of mud and wood
1038.hook: Djenné in Mali, wooden mosques in China and Java
1038.howItsDone: Muslims pray in mosques of every style and material, and when no mosque is near they pray on any clean ground or a prayer mat, facing the direction of Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Aqsa, the Far Distant Place of Worship in Jerusalem. Your line was the farthest mosque. When the city came up, did you pause and wish it peace? Day one thousand thirty-eight.

Three roofs. The first is flat, on walls of sun-dried mud bristling with wooden poles, in Djenné, in Mali. The second curves up at the corners like a temple roof, painted beams under clay tiles, in a courtyard in China. The third is stacked in layers, roof on roof on roof, a tall wooden pyramid in Java, in Indonesia. No dome on any of them. No tall pencil minaret. And all three are mosques, where people line up in rows and bow toward Mecca. How can three buildings look so unlike each other and do the same thing? Today: mosques of mud and wood.
screen: `A ROOF OF MUD IN MALI.` → `A TEMPLE ROOF IN CHINA.` → `A STACKED ROOF IN JAVA.`

segments.voice: The answer starts with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, he counts the things given to him, and one of them is this: the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for him and his community. Wherever the time of prayer finds you, you can pray there. So a mosque, at its simplest, is a clean place set apart, with the direction of Mecca marked. Everything else, the walls, the roof, the shape, is left to the builders. And builders use what they have. Second, the mud. We met Djenné earlier this year, the town that replasters its mosque together. Look this time at the method. In a land of river clay and heat, thick mud walls help keep a building cool, and the wooden poles in them give the plasterers a foothold when the walls are renewed. The material is local; so is the work. Third, the wood in China. Some old Chinese mosques were built in the style of Chinese halls: courtyards, gates, timber halls, curved roofs, inscriptions in Arabic and in Chinese characters side by side. A visitor might take one for a temple until the rows begin. Fourth, Java. Some of the old mosques there have tiered roofs carried on great wooden pillars, the way halls were raised on that island. There's a story people tell in Demak about one of those pillars, said to be pieced together from leftover wood chips by a saintly teacher. It's a story, not a record, but it shows how dearly the building is loved. The Qur'an says God made people "nations and tribes that ye may know one another." The mosques look like their nations. The rows inside look the same.
screen: `THE WHOLE EARTH IS A PLACE OF PRAYER.` · `MUD IN MALI, FROM THE RIVER.` · `TIMBER AND CURVED ROOFS IN CHINA.` · `TIERED ROOFS ON PILLARS IN JAVA.` · then, large: `NATIONS AND TRIBES THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: build a mosque in your mind out of what's around you. Settle, and breathe. Look at the room you're in, or remember the place you grew up. What would a house of prayer be made of there? Brick, stone, timber, glass, adobe, the gray concrete of a city block? What would keep it cool, or warm? Where would the light come in? Let it take shape slowly, wall by wall. Last of all, choose one wall and give it a small mark for the direction of prayer. That mark is the one thing every mosque shares. If you pray, you can bring that house into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Djenné, the Malian town whose mud mosque has thick walls for the heat and wooden poles that give plasterers a foothold when it's renewed. Today's word.
Your line: every land builds its own. Today, look up one mosque that surprises you, a roof or a wall you'd never have guessed, and notice what it's made of. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

1039.title: Istiqlal and Sheikh Zayed
1039.hook: great modern mosques in Jakarta and Abu Dhabi
1039.howItsDone: Large modern mosques often host Friday prayer, Ramadan night prayers and Eid gatherings, and some, like Sheikh Zayed in Abu Dhabi, welcome visitors with guided tours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mosques of mud and wood, in Mali's Djenné, in China and in Java. Your line was every land builds its own. Which mosque surprised you? Day one thousand thirty-nine.

Jakarta, Friday, noon. Traffic thick on the roads, motorbikes threading between buses, and in the middle of it all a vast white mosque with a broad dome and a single tall minaret. Its name is one word: Istiqlal. Independence. Across the road stands a Catholic cathedral with tall, pointed spires. Now cross an ocean to Abu Dhabi: a mosque of white marble, domes like clustered pearls, flowers of colored stone set into the floors, and tour groups of every faith walking through in the late afternoon. Two mosques, both raised in living memory. Today: Istiqlal and Sheikh Zayed.
screen: `JAKARTA: A MOSQUE CALLED INDEPENDENCE.` → `A CATHEDRAL ACROSS THE ROAD.` → `ABU DHABI: WHITE MARBLE, OPEN DOORS.`

segments.voice: First, the name in Jakarta. Istiqlal is the Arabic word for independence, and the mosque was planned as the national mosque of a newly independent Indonesia. A country that had just won its freedom chose to say so with a house of prayer. Second, the architect. The design that was chosen came from Friedrich Silaban, an Indonesian architect who was a Christian. A Christian drew the plans for the national mosque, and the mosque stands across from the cathedral. Some Indonesians point to that pair as a picture of neighbors living side by side. Third, Abu Dhabi. The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque carries the name of Sheikh Zayed, the leader who founded the United Arab Emirates, and he is buried beside it. Its builders gathered marble, stone, glass and craftsmen from many countries, and the mosque keeps its doors open to visitors of every faith, with guides to explain what they're seeing. Fourth, why build at all, when the whole earth is already a place of prayer? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that whoever builds a mosque, seeking the face of God, God builds for him a house like it in Paradise. And the Qur'an speaks of who truly keeps a mosque alive. In Pickthall's translation: "He only shall tend Allah's sanctuaries who believeth in Allah and the Last Day." Marble and domes are one thing. Tending is another: the people who pray there, sweep there, teach there. The Ka'ba, Medina, Jerusalem, Djenné, Jakarta, Abu Dhabi: every one of them was once new, and once built today.
screen: `ISTIQLAL MEANS INDEPENDENCE.` · `A CHRISTIAN DREW THE PLANS.` · `SHEIKH ZAYED: DOORS OPEN TO ALL.` · `A HOUSE BUILT, A HOUSE IN PARADISE.` · then, large: `HE ONLY SHALL TEND ALLAH'S SANCTUARIES.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at a modern mosque, slowly, as if you were walking through it. Settle, and breathe. If you have a screen nearby, find a photo of Istiqlal or Sheikh Zayed; if not, picture one of them. Start at the gate. Cross the courtyard. Notice the light on the floor, the pattern on a wall, the place where shoes are left in rows. Go inside, and stand where the prayer rows begin. Somebody laid that floor. Somebody cleans it tonight. If you pray, you can remember the builders and the sweepers in your prayer. If not, simply thank them in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Istiqlal, Indonesia's word for independence and the name its people gave the national mosque a Christian architect designed in Jakarta. Today's word.
Your line: built today. Today, notice one thing someone built recently for others to use, a bench, a ramp, a playground, and thank whoever made it. Day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: Your nearest mosque
1040.hook: every mosque is linked to the first
1040.howItsDone: Muslims pray in the nearest mosque when they can, especially for Friday prayer, facing the mihrab toward Mecca; some mosques also welcome visitors and hold open days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Istiqlal in Jakarta and Sheikh Zayed in Abu Dhabi, a mosque named independence and a mosque with open doors. Your line was built today. What did someone build that you used? Day one thousand forty.

Somewhere near where you're sitting, there may well be a mosque. It might have a dome. It might be a converted shop with a hand-painted sign, a room above a pharmacy, a prayer space in a hospital basement or a university hallway. You may have walked past it without ever looking up. Inside, on the front wall, there's very likely a small arched niche, or just a mark, showing which way to face. That mark is a thread. Pull it, and it runs across roads, seas and deserts, all the way to one house in Mecca. Today, the last of our houses of prayer: your nearest mosque.
screen: `A DOME, A SHOP, A BASEMENT ROOM.` → `A NICHE ON THE FRONT WALL.` → `A THREAD TO MECCA.`

segments.voice: First, the thread. The niche is called the mihrab, and the direction it shows is the qibla, the direction of the Ka'ba. The Qur'an tells the believers that wherever they are, they turn their faces toward the Sacred Mosque in prayer. So the smallest prayer room and the grandest hall point the same way. Second, the first house. Five days ago we heard the Qur'an call the house at Becca "the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind." A shop-front prayer room in a city you've never seen is turned toward that same house. That's what our line means: linked to the first. Third, the way in. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that whoever enters a mosque should pray two units of prayer before sitting down, a greeting for the house itself. Visitors who aren't Muslim aren't asked to pray, of course. Shoes come off at the door, people dress modestly, and a quiet hello goes a long way. Some mosques hold open days and welcome questions. Fourth, the blessing. Four days ago, in Medina, we heard the verse that asks believers to send blessings on the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Those blessings are called salawat, and some Muslims say them as they step into a mosque. Now look back. This long stretch of the path walked through history and civilization: caliphs and scholars, libraries and soup kitchens, empires, colonial rule, migration, and these houses of prayer. Mecca, Medina, Jerusalem, mud and wood, Jakarta and Abu Dhabi, and the one down your street. Next comes a new camp: the holy days in history.
screen: `THE MIHRAB SHOWS THE QIBLA.` · `THE FIRST SANCTUARY, AT BECCA.` · `A GREETING FOR THE HOUSE.` · `BLESSINGS ON THE PROPHET.` · then, large: `LINKED TO THE FIRST.`

segments.voice: The practice: send salawat for your nearest mosque. Settle, and breathe. Bring that mosque to mind, or, if you don't know one, the streets around you where one might be. Don't go inside this time. Stand across the road, in your mind, and watch the door. People come and go: someone early, someone late, someone holding a child's hand. With each person who goes in, breathe out slowly. If you pray, you can send salawat on the Prophet, in the words you know, once for each of them. If not, simply wish that house and its people well. The bell holds the time.
Qibla, the direction of prayer toward the Ka'ba, that every mosque's mihrab, however small or grand, points its worshippers to face. Today's word.

Your line: linked to the first. Today, find out whether your nearest mosque has an open day or a visitors' hour, and note it down, or walk past once and give the house a quiet hello. Day one thousand forty.

1041.title: Ramadan: the lanterns
1041.hook: Cairo's Ramadan lanterns, a custom centuries old
1041.howItsDone: In Egypt and in some families elsewhere, Ramadan lanterns are hung in streets, shop doorways and homes for the month, and children carry small ones in the evenings.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the houses of prayer with your nearest mosque, its niche, the mihrab, pointing along the qibla to Mecca. Your line was linked to the first. Did you find a visitors' hour, or pass by and say hello? Day one thousand forty-one.

A Cairo alley, just after sunset, in the month of fasting. Strings of lights zigzag between balconies. In a shop doorway hang lanterns in rows: tin frames punched with patterns, panes of red, green and blue glass, a little door on the side for the candle. A child walks past swinging a small one, singing. Some of the newer ones are plastic and play a tune when you press a button. The old ones smell of hot metal and wax. The whole street glows like the inside of a jewel box. A new camp starts today, the holy days in history, and it opens with one object. Today's word: fanous.
screen: `A CAIRO ALLEY AFTER SUNSET.` → `TIN, COLORED GLASS, A CANDLE.` → `A NEW CAMP: THE HOLY DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Fanous is the Arabic word for a lantern, and in Egypt it has come to mean the Ramadan lantern above all. Second, the story. There's a story people tell in Cairo about where the custom began. A Fatimid ruler, they say, arrived in the city by night, and the people came out to greet him carrying lanterns to light his way, and the lanterns stayed with the month. Other versions put the lanterns in the hands of children, or of women walking out after dark in the fasting month. Nobody can prove which is true. What the stories agree on is light, and Ramadan nights. Third, why light belongs here. The Qur'an names the month itself: "The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind." A month of revelation. And elsewhere the Qur'an gives a picture made of light. In Pickthall's translation: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The similitude of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp. The lamp is in a glass. The glass is as it were a shining star." A lamp, in a glass, in a niche. Some readers hear that verse in the glow of a fanous. Fourth, the street. Ramadan nights are busy: the meal at sunset, the night prayers, visits to family, a late walk. The fanous turns the dark street into a place to be. In homes far from Egypt, some families hang one by the door, or put one on the iftar table, so the children know the month has come.
screen: `FANOUS: THE ARABIC FOR LANTERN.` · `A STORY OF LIGHTS FOR A RULER.` · `A LAMP IN A GLASS, IN A NICHE.` · `THE DARK STREET BECOMES A PLACE.` · then, large: `ALLAH IS THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with one small light. If you can, light a candle, switch on a lamp, or simply look at the nearest glowing thing, a screen dimmed low, a streetlight through the window. Settle, and breathe. Watch the light for a while. Notice its edge, where it meets the dark. Notice how a small flame makes a room feel held. Let your breathing slow until the light seems steady. If you pray, you can recall the verse of light, a lamp in a glass, in a niche. If not, just rest your eyes on the glow. The bell holds the time.
Fanous. The lantern, and in Egypt above all the Ramadan lantern of tin and colored glass, carried through the streets after sunset. Today's word.
Your line: lanterns for ramadan. Tonight, when the light goes, light one lamp or candle on purpose and let it burn while you eat. Day one thousand forty-one.

1042.title: Ramadan: the iftar cannon
1042.hook: in some cities a cannon marks sunset for breaking the fast
1042.howItsDone: Muslims fasting in Ramadan break the fast at the call to the maghrib prayer, at sunset or, in Shia practice, a little after, often with dates and water; in some cities a cannon is fired at that moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fanous, the Ramadan lantern of tin and colored glass. Your line was lanterns for ramadan. Did you light a lamp on purpose last night? Day one thousand forty-two.

Late afternoon in the fasting month. A table is laid: dates in a bowl, water in glasses, soup keeping warm, a plate nobody is allowed to touch yet. Children hover. Somebody checks the window. Somebody else checks a phone. Everyone is listening. Then, from the hill across the city, a deep boom rolls over the rooftops, and the whole house moves at once. A date. A sip of water. Someone laughs. In some cities, that boom is the sound of sunset in Ramadan. Today: the iftar cannon.
screen: `DATES, WATER, AND WAITING.` → `A BOOM FROM THE HILL.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE MOVES AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, what the cannon is answering. The Qur'an sets the edges of the fasting day: eat and drink until the dawn is clear, and then, in Pickthall's translation, "Then strictly observe the fast till nightfall." In Sunni practice the fast ends at sunset, with the call to the sunset prayer; in Shia practice, a little later, when the redness has left the eastern sky. Before clocks on every wrist, a whole city needed to know the same moment at the same time. A call from a minaret carries only so far. A cannon carries much farther. Second, the story. There's a story people tell in Cairo, in several versions: a ruler was testing a new cannon, and by chance it fired just at sunset in Ramadan. The people took it as a signal, and thanked him, and so the firing became a custom. Whether it happened that way, nobody can say. But the custom spread, and in some cities a cannon still fires at sunset in Ramadan, sometimes carried on television and radio. Third, the hurry. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says people will remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast. Not lingering, not proving how long you can last. When the time comes, eat. The Qur'an gives the fast a firm edge at both ends, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asked people not to blur the second one. Fourth, the joy. Another hadith says the one who fasts has two joys: one when breaking the fast, and one on meeting the Lord. The cannon is the sound of the first joy, heard by a whole city at once.
screen: `STRICTLY OBSERVE THE FAST TILL NIGHTFALL.` · `A CANNON FIRED BY CHANCE, THEY SAY.` · `HURRY TO BREAK THE FAST.` · `TWO JOYS FOR THE ONE WHO FASTS.` · then, large: `THE CANNON AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: The practice: wait for a signal, and then answer it. Settle, and breathe. For the next stretch, simply listen to whatever sounds are around you: traffic, a fridge, a bird, your own breath. Don't do anything with them. Just wait, the way a family waits at the table. When the bell comes, let it be your cannon: take one slow sip of water and notice it. If you're fasting today, you can let this remind you to break the fast on time, without delay. If you pray, you can give thanks in the words you know. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The month of fasting from dawn to nightfall, and in some cities, the month a cannon tells everyone at once that the sun is down. Today's word.
Your line: the cannon at sunset. Today, whatever you're waiting for, when it arrives, take it gladly and without delay. Day one thousand forty-two.

1043.title: Ramadan: the drummer
1043.hook: a drummer walks the streets before dawn to wake people for suhur
1043.howItsDone: In parts of Egypt and other Muslim-majority lands, a musaharati still walks the streets before dawn in Ramadan with a small drum, calling households by name to wake for suhur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iftar cannon, one boom to tell a whole city the fast is over. Your line was the cannon at sunset. What did you take gladly, and without delay? Day one thousand forty-three.

Tap. Tap-tap. Tap. It's the dark hour before dawn in a Ramadan street, and the only sound is a small drum. A man walks under the balconies with a lantern and a stick, striking a little drum slung at his side. He stops at a door and calls a name. Not a general shout: a name. The son of the baker. The widow on the second floor. Upstairs, a light goes on. Then another. A child at a window waves, and he waves back without missing a beat. He walks on to the next street. Today's word is what people call him: musaharati.
screen: `A DRUM BEFORE DAWN.` → `HE CALLS YOU BY NAME.` → `ONE LIGHT, THEN ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the job. The musaharati, as he's called in Egypt, wakes people for suhur, the meal eaten in the dark before the fast begins at dawn. Other places have other names for the same work. Second, the chant. As he walks, he calls out lines inviting the sleeper to wake and to declare God one, and then he adds the names of the households. That last part is the heart of it. A whole street, known by name, woken one door at a time. Third, a waking call in Medina. Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tell that in the Prophet's own city, peace be upon him, Bilal used to call out while it was still night, so that sleepers would wake. The Prophet told the people that Bilal's call did not mean the fast had begun: keep eating and drinking until Ibn Umm Maktum calls, for he calls at dawn. Two voices, one to wake, one to mark the start. Fourth, the gentleness. Nobody wants to be shaken awake. The musaharati comes with rhythm, a lantern and your own name, and he's gone before you're cross. Today alarms and phones often do the job, yet in some neighborhoods the drummer still walks, and children still wait at the window for him. Look back at this week: the farthest mosque in Jerusalem; mosques of mud and wood, Djenné; mosques built today; your nearest mosque, and its qibla; then Ramadan, with its lanterns, its cannon, and now its drummer. Places, then nights.
screen: `HE WAKES THE STREET FOR SUHUR.` · `WAKE, SLEEPER, AND DECLARE GOD ONE.` · `BILAL CALLS BY NIGHT.` · `A RHYTHM, A LANTERN, YOUR NAME.` · then, large: `WAKE FOR SUHUR.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about how you wake people. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you wake, or someone you'll speak to first tomorrow: a child, a partner, a parent, a roommate, a colleague at the first meeting. How do you usually do it? A shout up the stairs? A text? Now try it the drummer's way, in your mind: a soft knock, their name said kindly, a little patience while they come round. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. If not, simply wish them a good morning before it comes. The bell holds the time.
Musaharati. The Ramadan drummer who walks the streets before dawn, calling each house by name to wake for suhur. Today's word.
Your line: wake for suhur. Tomorrow morning, wake someone gently, with their name and a little patience, the way the drummer would. Day one thousand forty-three.
